The term survives from naval practice (and lives on in 'nautical dawn' briefings) — the calculator keeps the tradition computable.
Sunrise is about 05:24; nautical dawn starts near 04:08 — roughly 76 minutes earlier. In midwinter the same gap is about 64 minutes (nautical dawn ~06:12 before a 07:16 sunrise).

At London's latitude the Sun dips so shallowly in June that nautical twilight can last all night around the solstice — astronomical darkness vanishes entirely, a fact the calculator shows rather than smooths over.

faq: The periods at dawn and dusk when the Sun's centre is between 6 and 12 degrees below the horizon — dark enough for the brighter stars used in celestial navigation, light enough to see the sea horizon.
The 6/12/18-degree ladder of civil, nautical and astronomical twilight is the international convention, inherited from nautical almanac practice.
At mid-latitudes, roughly an hour to ninety minutes each end of the day near the equinoxes, stretching toward the poles and shrinking near the equator — the calculator gives your place's real figure.
Can nautical twilight last all night?
Yes — poleward of about 48.6° latitude at the summer solstice the Sun never dips 12° below the horizon, so dusk runs straight into dawn.
Is it dark enough for stargazing?
Mostly — bright planets and major constellations show well; faint deep-sky work wants astronomical darkness, one rung deeper.
Does it give both dawn and dusk?
Yes — morning nautical dawn (when twilight begins) and evening nautical dusk (when it ends), for your date and coordinates.
A sextant needs stars and a horizon in the same eyepiece — that overlap exists only during nautical twilight, which is why the almanac prints it.
